newsitem.title: MALAWI: Malawi economy saw strong growth in 1996 - Muluzi.
newsitem.headline: Malawi economy saw strong growth in 1996 - Muluzi.

text.p: Malawi's economy saw strong growth in 1996 as gross domestic product (GDP) rose 9.7 percent on the back of a healthy agricultural sector, President Bakili Muluzi said on Wednesday.

"The strong performance in 1996 stems largely from the outstanding performance in agriculture production of 29.2 percent. This came largely from the smallholder subsector, which grew by close to 40 percent," Muluzi told the opening session of Malawi's new parliament in Zomba, about 60km north-east of the commercial capital Blantyre.
Muluzi said provisional estimates showed there would be a budget deficit excluding grants of 3,024.67 million kwacha ($198.47 million) in 1996/97, down from 3,427.00 million kwacha in 1995/96.
The budget deficit after grants would be 1,391.42 million kwacha in 1996/97, down from 1,414.00 million kwacha in 1995/96.

However, the session was overshadowed by the presence of only eight politicians on the opposition benches. Both main opposition parties are boycotting parliament in protest against Muluzi's appointment of six opposition members to his cabinet without consulting their parties' bosses.

Muluzi called for the Malawi Congress Party (MCP) and Alliance for Democracy (AFORD) to return to the chamber. He said they could make a more significant contribution in parliament than outside on the streets.

"I find it ironic that while several African countries are experiencing civil strifes because the opposition is blocked from entering parliament, here in Malawi the opposition is deliberately staying away from parliament," he said.
The opposition in Malawi started boycotting parliament in June last year.

The Malawi constitution provides that there be, at the beginning of each parliamentary session, a quorum of 118 members which constitute a two-thirds majority in the 177-member parliament. The ruling UDF party has 85 members.
But on Tuesday the Malawi High Court ruled that parliament could meet despite the boycott.
